stops.title: Torrey Landing

labels.text: 780 nests on the beaches this summer

rooms.title: A naturalist's field kit
rooms.alt: Watercolor still life on weathered dock boards: an open field journal with a painted map of Ossabaw and notes about a loggerhead hatchling, an indigo-dyed cloth, a block of tabby studded with oyster shells, a palmetto frond, oyster shells, binoculars, a live oak sprig with acorns and a sea turtle nest stake.
rooms.text: Each object on the dock stands for something you will meet on the island.

spots.title: The island in one page
spots.text: Ossabaw covers about 26,000 acres: 9,000 acres of high ground and 17,000 acres of salt marsh, 10 miles long and 7 miles wide.

spots.title: Indigo
spots.text: Indigo has grown wild by the Club House since colonial times. Enslaved Africans brought the knowledge of growing and processing it, and the Foundation teaches indigo dyeing each September.

spots.title: A block of tabby
spots.text: Lime, sand, water and oyster shell, poured in layers. The North End stop shows the cabins built from it.

spots.title: Cabbage palm
spots.text: One of the few palms native to the Southeast. The Torreys lined the causeway from the landing with them after they bought the island.

spots.title: Oyster shells
spots.text: The salt marsh is a nursery for oysters, blue crabs and fish. Shell heaps left by Indigenous people were later mined for tabby.

spots.title: A nest stake
spots.text: Each summer monitors mark loggerhead nests on the beach. Ossabaw counted 780 nests in 2026.

spots.title: Binoculars
spots.text: Audubon named Ossabaw an Important Bird Area in 2007. Wood storks, painted buntings and oystercatchers nest here.

spots.title: Live oak
spots.text: Georgia's state tree. Enslaved men cut Ossabaw's curved live oak limbs for the hulls of colonial ships.

stops.intro: Every visit starts here at the north end, after about 1 hour on the water. Unpack the naturalist's kit on the dock: each object stands for something you will meet on the island.

stops.title: The Main Road

rooms.title: The Main Road
rooms.alt: Watercolor of a sand road running under an avenue of live oaks hung with Spanish moss, a stone mile marker on the verge and a ditch alongside.
rooms.text: A sand road under live oaks, the oldest route on the island.

spots.title: An Indigenous path
spots.text: The Main Road began as an Indigenous path. A colonial survey map labels it "Indian Path". It runs 6 miles along the island's spine.

spots.title: Stone mile markers
spots.text: Stone markers along the road may date from just after 1776, when John Morel Sr.'s sons divided the island.

spots.title: The avenue
spots.text: Trees along the road were planted in the 1800s, and the Torreys kept them.

spots.title: Roads and ditches
spots.text: Enslaved laborers built and kept up the island's roads, ditches and causeways until emancipation.

spots.title: Toward Middle Place
spots.text: 2 miles down the road from Torrey Landing, Middle Place held a Guale village, a plantation, a freedpeople's church and, from 1970, the Genesis Project.

stops.intro: People have walked this road for 5,000 years. Tap the road, the oaks and the stone marker.

strip.v: Spanish soldiers burn the Guale village of Asapo.
John Morel takes over the island; the first record of enslaved Africans here.
Sea Island cotton replaces indigo on four plantations.
Freedpeople claim land under Sherman's field order; it is revoked the next year.
Hurricanes drive families to the mainland, where they found Pin Point.
Dr. Henry Norton Torrey and Nell Ford Torrey buy the island.
The Ossabaw Island Project opens to artists, writers and scientists.
Ossabaw becomes Georgia's first Heritage Preserve.

stops.title: The tabby cabins

rooms.title: A tabby cabin
rooms.alt: Watercolor of a tabby cabin under live oaks: gray shell-studded walls, a wood shingle roof, a central chimney and two doors, one for each family, with two more cabins beyond.
rooms.text: Two one-room homes back to back, split by a central chimney.

spots.title: Tabby walls
spots.text: Oyster shell, lime, sand and water, poured course by course. The pour lines still show.

spots.title: The central chimney
spots.text: One chimney heats both rooms, a plan called a saddlebag. Each cabin is about 400 sq ft.

spots.title: A door for each family
spots.text: Enslaved families lived on each side of the chimney. Their descendants lived here well into the 1900s.

spots.title: The roof
spots.text: Wood shingles over a simple gable.

spots.title: A row of cabins
spots.text: 3 cabins survive of perhaps 9 buildings. Two were restored in 2005 with a $400K Save America's Treasures grant and private gifts.

spots.title: Shuttered windows
spots.text: Small windows with wooden shutters let in light and air.

stops.intro: Three tabby cabins survive at the North End, built between 1820 to 1840 by enslaved carpenters and masons.

strip.v: Oyster shells are burned with wood into lime.
Lime, sand, water and whole shells make a thick paste.
The mix goes between wooden boards and is tamped down.
When a course sets, the boards move up for the next.

stops.title: The Torrey West House

rooms.title: The entrance front
rooms.alt: Watercolor of the Torrey West House: pink stucco walls, red barrel-tile roofs, a tiled arched doorway with lanterns, under live oaks hung with Spanish moss.
rooms.text: Savannah architect Henrik Wallin designed the house for Dr. Henry Norton Torrey and Nell Ford Torrey of Detroit as a winter home. Work began in 1924 and ended in 1926. Pink stucco, clay tile and iron gave it the look of the Mediterranean, and fire would find little to burn.

spots.title: The tiled doorway
spots.text: Glazed tiles of green and blue vines, edged in gold, frame the arched entry. A tile panel of an urn spilling foliage fills the arch above the door.

spots.title: Iron lanterns
spots.text: Black iron lanterns flank the door. The state's $7M rehabilitation restored them along with the stucco, woodwork and window grates; the facade work was done in 2026.

spots.title: Terra-cotta roof
spots.text: Red clay barrel tiles from Ludowici, Georgia, cover hipped roofs at several heights. The Ossabaw Island Foundation restored the roof in 2014.

spots.title: Iron balcony
spots.text: Small balconies on scrolled iron brackets hang under the upper windows, as they do in a 1926 photograph of the house.

spots.title: Window grates
spots.text: Iron grates with scrolled crests guard the tall ground-floor windows.

spots.title: Live oaks and moss
spots.text: Live oaks, Georgia's state tree, shade the lawn. Nell Torrey was a keen gardener, and acres of gardens once surrounded the house.

rooms.title: The Great Room
rooms.alt: Watercolor of the Great Room: dark paneled walls, timber trusses, an iron ring chandelier, a gallery with turned balusters, a stair with an iron rail, and a wide picture window over a cushioned seat.
rooms.text: The heart of the house faces Ossabaw Sound. The Torreys gathered guests here, and from 1961 the artists, writers and scientists of the Ossabaw Island Project shared their work here at the end of the day.

spots.title: Timber trusses
spots.text: Exposed timber trusses carry the roof over a room two stories tall.

spots.title: The gallery
spots.text: A second-floor gallery with turned balusters looks down on the room.

spots.title: Iron-railed stair
spots.text: A stair with an iron railing climbs to the gallery.

spots.title: Ring chandelier
spots.text: Iron ring chandeliers hold rows of candle lights.

spots.title: Wide plank floors
spots.text: Wide wooden planks run the length of the room.

rooms.title: The picture window
rooms.alt: Watercolor view from the window seat: Ossabaw Sound, low green islands on the horizon, golden marsh, and pelicans gliding.
rooms.text: Dr. Torrey called it a picture window in 1925. The tour calls it America's first. Nell Torrey's grandfather, John Baptiste Ford, founded the Pittsburgh Plate Glass Company.

spots.title: Ossabaw Sound
spots.text: The Sound separates Ossabaw from Wassaw Island to the north. The Ogeechee River empties into it.

spots.title: Raccoon Key
spots.text: A small island in Ossabaw Sound, part of the view Dr. Torrey framed.

spots.title: Wassaw Island
spots.text: The southern tip of Wassaw, another of Georgia's barrier islands without a bridge.

spots.title: Salt marsh
spots.text: Smooth cordgrass grows where the tide floods twice a day.

rooms.title: The dining room
rooms.alt: Watercolor of the dining room: cream plaster walls over colorful glazed tiles, painted ceiling beams, a herringbone terracotta floor, a long table and a tiled bay window seat.
rooms.text: The dining room is the most Spanish room in the house: plaster walls, a polychromed wood ceiling and detailed tile work.

spots.title: Painted ceiling
spots.text: Dark beams carry painted bands of red, blue and gold.

spots.title: Glazed tile
spots.text: Glazed tiles line the lower walls.

spots.title: Bay window seat
spots.text: A tiled seat fills the bay window.

spots.title: Herringbone floor
spots.text: Terracotta tiles laid in a herringbone pattern.

rooms.title: The butler's pantry
rooms.alt: Watercolor of the butler's pantry: green glass-front cabinets full of china, wood counters, a deep sink under a window, and a black-and-white checkerboard floor.
rooms.text: The pantry sits between the kitchen and the dining room. Staff staged meals here and kept the china and silver.

spots.title: Glass-front cabinets
spots.text: Green cabinets with glass doors show stacks of china.

spots.title: Deep sink
spots.text: A deep sink under the window, for washing the good china by hand.

spots.title: Wood counters
spots.text: Long wooden counters for setting out each course.

spots.title: Checkerboard floor
spots.text: Black and white tiles laid as a checkerboard.

rooms.title: The rear patio
rooms.alt: Watercolor from under the rear loggia: three pink stucco arches frame a tiled patio, an octagonal glass-and-iron cage, an iron stair, live oaks and Ossabaw Sound.
rooms.text: Arches shelter the patio from the winter wind, and it catches the sun over Ossabaw Sound. A small "monkey cage" opens off the morning room, from the years the Torreys kept exotic animals.

spots.title: The loggia
spots.text: Round arches carry the upper floor and its iron balconies.

spots.title: The monkey cage
spots.text: An octagonal enclosure of glass and iron. The tour links the small cage off the morning room to the Torreys' exotic pets.

spots.title: Glass tank
spots.text: A small octagonal glass tank on a stone base.

spots.title: Outdoor iron stair
spots.text: An iron stair climbs from the patio to the floor above.

spots.title: The Sound
spots.text: Past the lawn, the marsh and Ossabaw Sound.

stops.title: Marsh to surf

actors.name: Bald eagle
actors.fact: Georgia DNR biologists keep watch on the bald eagles that nest on Ossabaw, as they do on its wood storks.

actors.name: Fiddler crab
actors.fact: A male waves one oversized claw to court females and warn off rivals. When the tide floods the marsh, fiddlers plug their burrows and wait. In spring and summer the island's hogs hunt them.

actors.name: Great egret
actors.fact: Tidal creeks feed the island's egrets, herons, ibis and wood storks. Its interior ponds hold heron rookeries.

actors.name: Bottlenose dolphin
actors.fact: Dolphins appear on a 1970s survey of Ossabaw's mammals. They ride the flood tide up the creeks to hunt fish in the drowned cordgrass.

actors.name: American alligator
actors.fact: Alligators share the island's brackish Graves Ponds with river otters, roseate spoonbills and wood storks.

actors.name: Roseate spoonbill
actors.fact: A spoonbill sweeps its flat bill side to side through shallow water, feeling for shrimp and small fish.

actors.name: Wood stork
actors.fact: Wood storks nest on Ossabaw, and the state monitors them. A stork feeds by touch: it holds its open bill in the water and snaps it shut on a fish.

actors.name: Ossabaw Island hog
actors.fact: Descended from pigs Spanish explorers turned loose in the 1500s. Island adults weigh 100 lb to 200 lb, small for a feral pig.

actors.name: Ossabaw Island hog
actors.fact: Descended from pigs Spanish explorers turned loose in the 1500s. Island adults weigh 100 lb to 200 lb, small for a feral pig.

actors.name: Ossabaw piglet
actors.fact: Sows can breed at six months and bear litters of 8 piglets to 12 piglets after about 115 days, up to two litters a year.

actors.name: White-tailed deer
actors.fact: Deer browse the forest understory. After the state began removing hogs, deer on the island grew heavier.

actors.name: Painted bunting
actors.fact: A Near Threatened songbird. Ossabaw's woods help support the eastern U.S. population.

actors.name: Free-range donkey
actors.fact: One of the 8 donkeys left on the island, all sterilized. Sandy West brought the first Sicilian donkeys in 1965.

actors.name: American oystercatcher
actors.fact: A beach-nesting bird of concern on Ossabaw. Its long red bill pries open oysters and clams.

actors.name: Sanderling
actors.fact: Low tide brings sanderlings, plovers, knots and turnstones to feed along the wet sand.

actors.name: Loggerhead hatchling
actors.fact: Hatchlings dig out together, usually at night, and run for the brightest horizon: the sea. Ossabaw beaches held 780 nests in 2026.

notes.text: Low tide. Mud banks and oyster beds lie open; fiddler crabs feed and wave, and sanderlings chase the surf.
The tide is coming in. The marsh floods twice a day, and the water climbs the creek banks first.
High tide. Water spills into the cordgrass and dolphins hunt up the creek, while the crabs wait out the flood in their burrows.

zones.label: Salt marsh
zones.text: Smooth cordgrass grows in the lowest marsh, where the tide floods twice a day. About 17,000 acres of marsh ring the island, a nursery for blue crabs and fish.

zones.label: Pond
zones.text: Brackish ponds such as the Graves Ponds hold alligators, river otters, roseate spoonbills and wood storks. Heron rookeries sit at the interior ponds.

zones.label: Maritime forest
zones.text: Live oaks, cabbage palms, magnolias and pines cover about 36% of the island, over thickets of saw palmetto.

zones.label: Old field
zones.text: Some meadows are natural; others are old cotton fields from the island's plantations. The DNR mows and burns them to keep them open.

zones.label: Dunes
zones.text: The dune ridges on the Atlantic side are younger than 4,000 years. Sea oats hold the sand; at Bradley Point the dunes rise about 30 feet.

zones.label: Beach
zones.text: About 13 miles of sand, reshaped every day by the waves. Loggerheads nest above the high-tide line from late May to mid-August.

stops.title: The nesting beach

steps.title: Late May, after dark
steps.text: A female loggerhead leaves the surf and drags herself up the beach, leaving a track like a tractor's.

steps.title: She digs
steps.text: Above the high-tide line she scoops a flask-shaped chamber with her rear flippers, as deep as her flippers reach.

steps.title: 100 eggs to 150 eggs eggs
steps.text: She lays a clutch of soft, leathery eggs the size of ping-pong balls, covers them, and crawls back to the sea before dawn.

steps.title: Morning: the nest is marked
steps.text: Monitors follow her track, confirm the eggs, and set a numbered stake and a wire screen to keep hogs and raccoons out.

steps.title: About 8 weeks in the sand
steps.text: The sand's warmth incubates the eggs. Warmer nests hatch more females, cooler nests more males.

steps.title: Hatching night
steps.text: The hatchlings break out together and dig upward as a group, then wait just under the surface until the sand cools after dark.

steps.title: The run for the sea
steps.text: They boil out of the sand and scramble toward the bright horizon over the water. Many years later, the females that survive return to nest on this coast.

stops.intro: Step through one loggerhead nest, from the night it is dug to the night the hatchlings run for the sea.

pins.title: Middle Place
pins.text: 2 miles down the Main Road: a Guale village, a cotton plantation, a freedpeople's church and, from 1970, the Genesis Project.

pins.title: Freshwater ponds
pins.text: In 1924 artesian wells fed 15 ponds. The wells stopped in the 1960s, and the ponds now fill with rain.

pins.title: Bradley Point
pins.text: Dunes here rise about 30 feet over Ossabaw Sound.

pins.title: Hunt Camp
pins.text: Georgia DNR's check-in station and dock on Newell Creek, where hunters land for the deer and hog hunts.

pins.title: South End
pins.text: The sea has cut into the forest here and left a bone yard of dead oaks and pines on the beach.

events.title: Spanish soldiers burn Asapo
events.text: The Guale village, probably on the south end, is destroyed. Spain never builds a mission on Ossabaw.

events.title: John Morel takes over the island
events.text: Morel buys 30 people, the earliest record of enslaved Africans on Ossabaw. When he died his estate listed 155 people enslaved people.

events.title: Cotton replaces indigo
events.text: Sea Island cotton becomes the main crop on four plantations: North End, Middle Place, South End and Buckhead.

events.title: Tabby cabins at the North End
events.text: Enslaved carpenters and masons build cabins of tabby between 1820 to 1840.

events.title: Sherman's field order
events.text: Freedpeople claim land on Ossabaw, 7 families at Middle Place. President Andrew Johnson revokes the order, and within a year and a half the land is back with its former owners.

events.title: Hinder Me Not Baptist Church
events.text: Freedman David Bond's church counts 68 members.

events.title: Hurricanes drive families off
events.text: After the storms of the 1890s most Black residents move to the mainland and found Pin Point, a Gullah Geechee community.

events.title: The Torreys buy Ossabaw
events.text: Dr. Henry Norton Torrey and Nell Ford Torrey of Detroit buy the island as a winter retreat and finish their house in 1926.

events.title: The Ossabaw Island Project
events.text: Sandy and Clifford West open the island to painters, writers, composers and scientists.

events.title: The Genesis Project
events.text: Students live and work at Middle Place with no running water or electricity.

events.title: Georgia's first Heritage Preserve
events.text: The family sells to the state for $8M, 50% of the appraised value.

events.title: Sandy West dies at 108 years old
events.text: She dies on her birthday, five years after leaving the island at 103 years old.

events.title: The house turns 100
events.text: The state finishes a $7M rehabilitation of the Torrey West House.

actors.fact: Georgia DNR biologists keep watch on the bald eagles that nest on Ossabaw, as they do on its wood storks.

actors.name: Fiddler crab
actors.fact: A male waves one oversized claw to court females and warn off rivals. When the tide floods the marsh, fiddlers plug their burrows and wait. In spring and summer the island's hogs hunt them.

actors.name: Great egret
actors.fact: Tidal creeks feed the island's egrets, herons, ibis and wood storks. Its interior ponds hold heron rookeries.

actors.name: Bottlenose dolphin
actors.fact: Dolphins appear on a 1970s survey of Ossabaw's mammals. They ride the flood tide up the creeks to hunt fish in the drowned cordgrass.

actors.name: American alligator
actors.fact: Alligators share the island's brackish Graves Ponds with river otters, roseate spoonbills and wood storks.

actors.name: Roseate spoonbill
actors.fact: A spoonbill sweeps its flat bill side to side through shallow water, feeling for shrimp and small fish.

actors.name: Wood stork
actors.fact: Wood storks nest on Ossabaw, and the state monitors them. A stork feeds by touch: it holds its open bill in the water and snaps it shut on a fish.

actors.name: Ossabaw Island hog
actors.fact: Descended from pigs Spanish explorers turned loose in the 1500s. Island adults weigh 100 lb to 200 lb, small for a feral pig.

actors.name: Ossabaw piglet
actors.fact: Sows can breed at six months and bear litters of 8 piglets to 12 piglets after about 115 days, up to two litters a year.

actors.name: White-tailed deer
actors.fact: Deer browse the forest understory. After the state began removing hogs, deer on the island grew heavier.

actors.name: Painted bunting
actors.fact: A Near Threatened songbird. Ossabaw's woods help support the eastern U.S. population.

actors.name: Free-range donkey
actors.fact: One of the 8 donkeys left on the island, all sterilized. Sandy West brought the first Sicilian donkeys in 1965.

actors.name: American oystercatcher
actors.fact: A beach-nesting bird of concern on Ossabaw. Its long red bill pries open oysters and clams.

actors.name: Sanderling
actors.fact: Low tide brings sanderlings, plovers, knots and turnstones to feed along the wet sand.

actors.name: Loggerhead hatchling
actors.fact: Hatchlings dig out together, usually at night, and run for the brightest horizon: the sea. Ossabaw beaches held 780 nests in 2026.

notes.text: Low tide. Mud banks and oyster beds lie open; fiddler crabs feed and wave, and sanderlings chase the surf.
The tide is coming in. The marsh floods twice a day, and the water climbs the creek banks first.
High tide. Water spills into the cordgrass and dolphins hunt up the creek, while the crabs wait out the flood in their burrows.

zones.label: Salt marsh
zones.text: Smooth cordgrass grows in the lowest marsh, where the tide floods twice a day. About 17,000 acres of marsh ring the island, a nursery for blue crabs and fish.

zones.label: Pond
zones.text: Brackish ponds such as the Graves Ponds hold alligators, river otters, roseate spoonbills and wood storks. Heron rookeries sit at the interior ponds.

zones.label: Maritime forest
zones.text: Live oaks, cabbage palms, magnolias and pines cover about 36% of the island, over thickets of saw palmetto.

zones.label: Old field
zones.text: Some meadows are natural; others are old cotton fields from the island's plantations. The DNR mows and burns them to keep them open.

zones.label: Dunes
zones.text: The dune ridges on the Atlantic side are younger than 4,000 years. Sea oats hold the sand; at Bradley Point the dunes rise about 30 feet.

zones.label: Beach
zones.text: About 13 miles of sand, reshaped every day by the waves. Loggerheads nest above the high-tide line from late May to mid-August.

steps.title: Late May, after dark
steps.text: A female loggerhead leaves the surf and drags herself up the beach, leaving a track like a tractor's.

steps.title: She digs
steps.text: Above the high-tide line she scoops a flask-shaped chamber with her rear flippers, as deep as her flippers reach.

steps.title: 100 eggs to 150 eggs eggs
steps.text: She lays a clutch of soft, leathery eggs the size of ping-pong balls, covers them, and crawls back to the sea before dawn.

steps.title: Morning: the nest is marked
steps.text: Monitors follow her track, confirm the eggs, and set a numbered stake and a wire screen to keep hogs and raccoons out.

steps.title: About 8 weeks in the sand
steps.text: The sand's warmth incubates the eggs. Warmer nests hatch more females, cooler nests more males.

steps.title: Hatching night
steps.text: The hatchlings break out together and dig upward as a group, then wait just under the surface until the sand cools after dark.

steps.title: The run for the sea
steps.text: They boil out of the sand and scramble toward the bright horizon over the water. Many years later, the females that survive return to nest on this coast.
